$comment: Shared plugin path-scope conformance table.
A plugin HTTP hook is scoped by path: `http.onRequest({ match })`,
`http.onResponse({ match })`, and `http.route({ path })` all decide whether
they run by comparing a pattern against 'the path of this request'. The
router answers that question with the canonical segment form. Until this
table existed the plugin stage answered it with the raw request target, so
`//api/users` routed to `/api/users` and read as out of scope for
`['/api/*']` — and `originGuard()`, whose default scope is exactly that
pattern, did not run for a plain cross-site form POST that reached the
same route handler with the session cookie attached.
Every host replays this file:
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/plugins.test.mjs   (deployed host: plugin-http.mjs)
- crates/ruvyxa_dev_server/src/plugin_bridge.rs   (native host: dev/start)
The two halves assert different things because the seam is in a different
place in each. The deployed host owns the whole decision: it drives
`matchesPatterns(decodedRequestPathname(request), patterns)` and the
`entry.path` comparison, so it asserts `canonical`, `inScope`, and
`matchesRoute`. The native host runs the same JavaScript registry in a
child process, so all it owns is *which path string it hands over*: it
asserts that the plugin request target carries `canonical`, and that a
`canonical: null` target is refused before the plugin stage is reached.
Add a case here first when changing path scoping; a host that drifts then
fails in the host that drifted, not in review.
$patternsComment: The two shapes `normalizePatterns` accepts: a trailing-`*` prefix and an
exact path. `originGuard()` defaults to the first.
$routePathComment: A `http.route({ path })` registration is compared by exact equality against
the same path string, not by pattern. It is in this table so the equality
and the pattern match cannot be canonicalised apart.
$casesComment: `target` is the raw request target a client can send. `canonical` is the
path the router resolves it to — `null` means the path is refused outright
(400), never matched. `inScope` is per key of `patterns`; `matchesRoute` is
When `canonical` is null the deployed host falls back to `fallbackPathname`
— the raw, undecoded pathname — because a hook that cannot be told the
canonical path must still run rather than be silently skipped. The native
host never reaches the plugin stage for those targets at all.

cases.$comment: The attack in RUV-C2: a cross-site form POST to //api/users.

$comment: A trailing-`*` pattern keeps the separator, so `/api/*` has never
covered the bare `/api` route handler. Pinned here because the
canonicalisation makes `/api/` answer the same way, which is a
narrowing against the raw comparison and the point of the table.
The narrowing named above. `/api/` routes to `/api`, so a hook scoped
to `/api/*` no longer runs for it — matching `/api` exactly, which the
same hook has always answered. A guard meant to cover the collection
endpoint itself lists `/api` alongside `/api/*`.

cases.$comment: Exact patterns widen: the trailing slash now reaches the guard.
An exact pattern still does not cover children.
Percent-decoding is per segment and unchanged by this table.
A plugin route answers the address the router sends to it.

$comment: An encoded separator would let one URL address a route it does not
name, so the router refuses it. The deployed host still runs the
guard against the raw pathname — failing open here would hand back
the bypass this table exists to close.
A control character in a decoded segment is refused for the same
reason. Traversal spellings such as `/admin/%2E%2E` are deliberately
absent: WHATWG `URL` resolves `%2E` as a dot segment, so the deployed
host reads that target as `/` before this seam is reached while the
native host still sees the encoded form — a URL-parsing difference
outside this table's subject, and one both hosts refuse either way.
